text: You just learned how to multiply a matrix by a vector. Now the key conceptual leap: a matrix isn't just a grid of numbers — it's a transformation, a rule that takes any vector in and produces a new vector out. Every quantum gate is literally this.

Feed a matrix every possible input vector and it defines one consistent geometric rule — stretching, rotating, or flipping space. The matrix that rotates a 2D vector counterclockwise by an angle theta is cosine theta, negative sine theta, sine theta, cosine theta. That one fixed rule, applied consistently to any vector, is exactly what lets us describe a quantum gate once, as a single matrix, and know it will act the same way on whatever state it's given.

At 90 degrees, cosine is 0 and sine is 1, so the rotation matrix becomes 0, negative 1, 1, 0. Apply it to the vector 1,0, pointing right, and it becomes 0,1, pointing straight up — rotated exactly 90 degrees. Apply the same matrix to a different vector, 2,1, and it becomes negative 1,2 — same rule, consistently applied to a new input.

The Pauli-X matrix is 0,1,1,0 — the quantum analog of a classical NOT gate. Multiply it by ket-zero, which is 1,0, and you get 0,1, which is ket-one. Multiply it by ket-one, 0,1, and you get 1,0, which is ket-zero. X flips ket-zero and ket-one — the identical row-times-column multiplication from last lesson, now applied to a physically meaningful qubit state.

Next lesson asks the reversibility question every quantum gate must answer: if you know the output state, can you always recover the input? The matrix inverse is the tool, and the determinant decides whether one exists.
